title: File systems: inodes, links and file descriptors
goal: By the end, you can explain why a file's name is only a label that points to it, predict what two programs writing to one file will do, find and rescue a deleted file that a program still has open, and fix the error "Too many open files".
opening:
Picture the small company whose program records card payments for coffee shops: who paid, which shop, how much. The program also writes a line about every payment to a log file, which has grown to 20 GB. One evening the disk it runs on is 98% full. Someone deletes the log. The file vanishes from every folder listing, and the disk is still 98% full.

It's easy to think a file is its name. A file browser shows it that way: one name, one icon, and delete takes both. Underneath, the name is only a label that points to the file, and a file can outlive its label.

In The page cache, writeback and fsync, one rename swapped a new file in under an old name. That works because a name and a file are separate things. In this lesson, we'll take a file apart, watch two programs write to one file, rescue a deleted file that a program still holds, and run a program out of open files. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: The payments program still has its log file open, and it keeps writing a line every second, when someone deletes the file. When do the 20 GB of disk space come back?
options: At once: the file is deleted, and the disk only needs a moment to catch up
When the program closes the file, for example when it restarts
Never, until someone runs a repair program on the disk
At the program's next write, which fails because the file is gone, so the program stops logging
warmup.why: Deleting a file removes a name. The kernel, the core of the operating system that manages files for every program, frees a file's space only when no name points to it and no program has it open. The payments program still has it open, so its new lines keep landing in a file that no folder lists, and the disk keeps counting all 20 GB. The program gets no error either, which rules out the last option: nothing tells it that the name has gone. The first option is the trap for anyone who thinks a file is its name. The third section finds such a file, rescues it and frees its space without a restart.

sections.h: Names and inodes: a file's name only points to it
sections.body:
Let's start with one small file. Linux is an operating system, the program that runs all the others. The lab box is a small Linux system that Docker, a free program, runs on your laptop. In it, the command `stat` prints what the system knows about a file. For ours it shows `Inode: 1573046` and `Links: 1`. Give the file a second name with `ln`, and `stat` on either name prints the same inode number and `Links: 2`. Two names, one file. To see why, start with what has to be stored.

A disk, the device that keeps data while the power is off, is a long row of equal pieces called blocks, 4 KB (4,096 bytes) each in this track. The file system is the part of the operating system that decides which blocks belong to which file. For every file, it must record which blocks hold the bytes, the size, the owner, who may read it and when it last changed.

The simplest design keeps all of that next to the name: one row per file, and a folder is a table of rows. It breaks on the first file you want under two names. Say the payments program writes the year's payments to `ledger.csv` (a ledger is a book of accounts), and an auditor wants the same 2 GB file as `ledger-2026.csv`, without a copy. Now two rows must agree forever. Add a payment through one name, and the other row's size is wrong.

Libraries solved this long ago. Each book has a number, and catalogue cards say "this title, book 13". One book can have a card under its title and one under its author, and neither card is the book.

Unix, the family of operating systems Linux belongs to, splits the row the same way. The **inode** (index node) is the file itself, like the numbered book: its type, size, owner, permissions, timestamps, a link count and the list of blocks that hold the data. It has a number and no name. A **directory**, Linux's word for a folder, is the catalogue: a file whose content is a list of entries, each a name and an inode number. To open `/tmp/ledger.csv`, the kernel, the core of the operating system, reads the top directory, `/`, to find `tmp` and its number. Then it reads `tmp` to find `ledger.csv` and its number, and then that inode.

A second name is a second entry with the same number. That's a **hard link**, and the link count says how many entries point at the inode. So `rm`, the delete command, doesn't really delete. It makes a system call (a request from a program to the kernel) named `unlink`, which removes one entry and lowers the count by one. The kernel frees the inode and its blocks when the count reaches 0 and, as the third section shows, no program still has the file open. A rename changes one entry and leaves the inode alone, which is how the last lesson swapped a file in one step.

A **symbolic link**, or symlink, is an inode of its own whose content is a path, the chain of folder names that leads to a file. `latest.csv` holds the 10 bytes `ledger.csv`, and the kernel looks that path up again every time the link is opened. It's the card that says "see under *Ledger*". Remove the name it points to, and the symlink leads nowhere, while a hard link keeps working.

A hard link holds only a number, so it can't reach into another file system, whose numbers mean something else. And Linux refuses hard links to directories, which could make loops in the tree of folders. Here the library picture breaks: a library has one flat catalogue, while folders sit inside folders. Next, we'll open a file and write to it.

try.title: Two names, one inode
steps: From the `labs` folder, start the lab box: `docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm box`.

The block makes a file, gives it a second name with `ln` (a hard link) and makes a symlink with `ln -s`. It prints their inode numbers and link counts, then deletes the first name. Predict what each `cat` (a command that prints a file) shows, and the link count after `rm`.
The last line uses `strace`, a tool that prints every system call a program makes, to show the calls behind `ln`, `ln -s`, `mv` (rename) and `rm`.

code.title: in the lab box
code.src:
cd /tmp
echo 'auth-7731,4111,120.00,approved' > ledger.csv
ln ledger.csv ledger-2026.csv
ln -s ledger.csv latest.csv
stat -c '%n: inode %i, %h links, %s bytes, %F' ledger.csv ledger-2026.csv latest.csv
rm ledger.csv
cat ledger-2026.csv
cat latest.csv
stat -c '%n: inode %i, %h links' ledger-2026.csv
strace -f -e trace=linkat,symlinkat,unlinkat,renameat2 sh -c 'ln ledger-2026.csv b.csv; ln -s b.csv c.csv; mv b.csv d.csv; rm d.csv c.csv' 2>&1 | grep -E 'link|rename'

Inode numbers differ on your machine:

```text

ledger-2026.csv: inode 1573046, 2 links, 31 bytes, regular file
latest.csv: inode 1573048, 1 links, 10 bytes, symbolic link

ledger-2026.csv: inode 1573046, 1 links
[pid    19] linkat(AT_FDCWD, "ledger-2026.csv", AT_FDCWD, "b.csv", 0) = 0
[pid    20] symlinkat("b.csv", AT_FDCWD, "c.csv") = 0
[pid    21] renameat2(AT_FDCWD, "b.csv", AT_FDCWD, "d.csv", RENAME_NOREPLACE) = 0
[pid    22] unlinkat(AT_FDCWD, "d.csv", 0) = 0
[pid    22] unlinkat(AT_FDCWD, "c.csv", 0) = 0

```

The hard link has the same inode number as the original, and the count is 2. The symlink has its own inode and is 10 bytes long: those bytes are the path `ledger.csv`. After `rm`, the data is still there through `ledger-2026.csv`, whose count dropped to 1. The symlink fails, because the name it holds is gone. (`cat`'s complaint prints last because it goes to a separate channel for errors.) The trace shows four calls: `linkat` adds an entry for an existing inode, `symlinkat` makes a new inode that holds a path, `renameat2` moves an entry and `unlinkat` removes one. None of them touches the file's data.

sections.h: Two programs, one file: where the write position lives
sections.body:
`share.c` is a small C program that makes the problem visible. It calls `fork`, the system call that copies a running program, or process: the copy is the child, and the original is the parent. The child writes three records to `auth.log`, then the parent writes three more. Run one way, the file ends with all six. Run another way, with exactly the same writes, it ends with the parent's three, and the child's are gone. No call fails. The difference is where the write position lives.

When a program opens a file, the kernel hands back a small number, the **file descriptor** (fd). The program passes it in every later call, like a ticket number at a counter. The first file usually gets 3, because 0, 1 and 2 are taken by standard input, output and error, which are usually the terminal window where you type commands. Every `read` and `write` through an fd moves an **offset**, the position where the next byte goes. Think of it as a bookmark.

The obvious design keeps the bookmark in the descriptor: each process has its own fds, each with its own offset. That design breaks the shell, the program that runs the commands you type. `(date; hostname) > out.txt` runs two programs one after the other and sends what they print to `out.txt`. The shell opened the file once, and both programs got it as fd 1 through `fork` and `exec`. (`exec` makes a process run a different program; Processes: fork, exec, wait and signals showed both.) With an offset each, starting at 0, `hostname` would write over `date`'s line. In fact you get both lines, one under the other.

So Linux keeps three tables. Each process has an **fd table** that maps its fd numbers to pointers. Each pointer leads to an **open file description**, made by one `open()` call, which holds the offset and the flags the file was opened with. The description points at the inode. `fork` copies the fd table, so the child's fd 3 reaches the parent's description, and the two share one bookmark. `dup2`, a call that copies one fd number onto another, does the same inside one process, and the shell uses it for `>`. A second `open()` of the same file makes a new description, with its own bookmark at 0. `/proc` is a folder the kernel fills with live facts about each running process, and `/proc/<pid>/fdinfo/<fd>` prints a description's `pos` (the offset) and `flags`. (`<pid>` is the process's number.)

That explains `share.c`. Open the file once before `fork`, and the child's writes move the shared offset to 42, so the parent writes from 42 and nothing is lost. Open it separately after `fork`, and the parent's description is still at 0, so its writes land on the child's bytes. The stepper walks through both.

Two programs that open one log file on their own need **`O_APPEND`**, a flag passed to `open()`. With it, the kernel moves the offset to the end of the file before every write, in the same step as the write, so no writer lands on another's bytes. Java's `FileOutputStream(file, true)` opens files this way, and so do Logback and Log4j, two libraries many Java programs log with. Keep one record per `write()` call, too. On Linux's local file systems, another writer can't split one write, but it can land between two.

**Two writers on one file will overwrite each other. Open it with `O_APPEND`.**

An fd, a description, an inode: `rm` removes none of them. Next, we'll delete a file while a program still holds it.

sections.h: Deleting a file that a program still has open
sections.body:
Now the opening's scene, in miniature. `LogHolder` is a small Java program that writes 40 MB to `/dev/shm/auth.log` and keeps logging into it. (`/dev/shm` is a small file system that lives in memory.) It runs in the JVM, the Java virtual machine, which is the program that runs Java code. Delete the file under it, and `df`, which reports how full a file system is, still says 41 MB are in use. `du`, which adds up the sizes of files, says 0.

Both are right. `du` walks directory entries and adds up the files they reach, and no entry reaches this inode any more. `df` asks the file system how many blocks are in use, and these still are. The rule from the first section has a second half: the kernel frees an inode when its link count is 0 **and** no open file description points at it. The JVM's fd 4 still points at a description, which points at the inode, so the program keeps writing into a file nobody can find by name. In the library, every catalogue card is gone, but a reader still has the book on their desk. It goes back into stock only when they return it.

You can find the file from the program's side. `/proc/<pid>/fd/` has one entry per descriptor, and for a file that has lost every name, it shows the old path followed by `(deleted)`. `lsof`, a tool that lists open files, finds them too: `lsof +L1` lists every open file with fewer than one link. The `/proc` entry also opens the file, so `cp /proc/<pid>/fd/4 recovered.log` copies all 40 MB back out, for as long as the program runs.

On a real computer, this shows up as a full disk nobody can explain. A cleanup job deletes old logs, or someone deletes a 20 GB log to make room, and the space comes back only when the program restarts. The fix without a restart is to truncate the file, which cuts it to 0 bytes and keeps it. Do it through its name (`: > app.log` is the shell's short way to empty a file) or, once the name is gone, through `/proc` (`: > /proc/<pid>/fd/4`), and `df` drops at once.

That works cleanly when the writer opened the file with `O_APPEND`, because its next write goes to the new end. A writer without it keeps its old bookmark, 40 MB in, and its next write leaves a 40 MB gap of zeros in front. The lasting fix is in how old logs get moved aside, which is called rotating them. Logback and Log4j can rename the old file and open a new one themselves. For a program that can't reopen its log, logrotate, a standard Linux tool for this job, has a `copytruncate` setting: copy the file, then truncate it in place.

**Deleting a file that's still open frees nothing. Truncate it instead.**

So far our programs held one or two descriptors. Next, we'll see what happens when a program never gives them back.

steps: `os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l10/demo/LogHolder.java` opens `/dev/shm/auth.log` in append mode, writes 40 MB and keeps logging a line a second. `/dev/shm` is a small in-memory file system in every container (the boxed-off Linux system that Docker runs), so `df` there shows only this file.

The block starts it in the background (the `&`), deletes the file while it runs, then looks at the file from `df`, `du`, `/proc` and `lsof`. It copies the file back, and frees the space by truncating it through `/proc`. Predict each `df` line before you run it.

sections.h: Too many open files: every file and connection uses a descriptor
sections.body:
`FdLeak` is a Java program with a bug on purpose: it opens a small file for every pretend request and never closes it. With the limit set to 256 descriptors, open number 253 fails with `java.io.FileNotFoundException: /etc/hostname (Too many open files)`. The JVM already had 4 open (0, 1, 2 and one file of Java's own, `lib/modules`), and 4 + 252 is 256.

An fd table can't grow forever, because every entry holds kernel memory. Behind each entry sit a description and a file, or a network connection's waiting bytes, or a pipe (a channel one program writes into and another reads from). So the kernel caps each table with a resource limit named `RLIMIT_NOFILE`, which the shell command `ulimit -n` sets. A process at its limit can't make a new descriptor. `open` fails with the error `EMFILE`, which Java reports as "Too many open files", and so do `socket`, `accept` and `pipe`, the calls that make connections and pipes.

The name misleads, because every network connection is a descriptor too. A program that keeps 20 connections open to a database holds 20, and a server, a program that answers many clients over the network, holds one for each client.

The limit has two values. The **soft** limit is the one the kernel enforces. A process may raise it up to the **hard** limit, and only a privileged process, one with the administrator's rights, can raise the hard one. The JVM raises it for you. At start-up, HotSpot (the JVM most people run) sets the soft limit to the hard one, through a setting called `MaxFDLimit` that's on by default. `strace` shows the two calls, and a JVM started under `ulimit -S -n 256` opened 5,000 files without trouble. So what limits a JVM is the hard limit: 1,048,576 in the lab box, Docker's default here. `grep 'open files' /proc/<pid>/limits` shows it for a running program.

A high limit doesn't fix a leak. It only moves the failure. Above every process sits a limit for the whole machine, `fs.file-max`, 812,037 in this Docker setup. An earlier version of `FdLeak` had no cap. It reached that limit after 810,087 opens and failed with "Too many open files in system" (`ENFILE`). For that moment, every other process on the machine was refused new files too, which is a rude thing for one program to do. `FdLeak` now stops at 5,000.

To watch a program, count its descriptors over time with `ls /proc/<pid>/fd | wc -l` (`wc -l` counts lines). A count that climbs with traffic and never comes back down is a leak: a file, a connection or a folder listing that nobody closed. In Java, `try (...)` closes it for you at the end of the block, and in Kotlin, `use {}` does.

**An unclosed descriptor is a leak, whatever the limit. Close it where you open it.**

The limits protect the kernel's memory. The last section protects the file system's own records, when the power fails halfway through a change.

aside.title: Why does a network connection count as an open file?
aside.body: Unix gives a program one way to work with anything it reads or writes through the kernel: a descriptor. A file, a network connection, a pipe between two programs and even the terminal window all get one, and `read` and `write` work on all of them. That keeps programs simple, because the same code can write to a file or to a connection. The price is one shared table with one limit. So a program that forgets to close its connections can fail to open its settings file, with an error that only talks about files.

sections.h: Surviving a power cut: how a journal keeps the disk consistent
sections.body:
Let's read an inode off a disk. ext4 is one of the most common Linux file systems, and `debugfs` reads one straight from a disk image, a single file that holds a whole pretend disk. For `ledger.csv` it prints `Inode: 13`, `Size: 31`, `Links: 2` and, under `EXTENTS`, `(0):2065`: block 0 of the file is block 2065 of the disk. That's the first section's inode, on disk.

Adding one block to a file changes at least three places on the disk. There's the new data block. There's the block bitmap, a row of bits, one per block, set while the block is in use. And there's the inode, which gets a new size and a new extent, a note of which disk blocks hold which part of the file. The disk writes them one at a time. Lose power between two writes, and the file system contradicts itself. A block marked as used that no inode owns is lost space. An inode that points at a block the bitmap still calls free is worse: the next file gets that block too, and two files share bytes.

The old fix was `fsck`, a program that reads every inode and every bitmap after a crash and repairs what disagrees. On a big disk that takes minutes to hours, and the computer can't start its programs until it's done.

Picture a librarian halfway through moving a book to a new shelf, with the shelf list, the book's record and the catalogue to change. If she's called away in the middle, the library is a mess. So first she writes the whole change in a notebook and signs it. After an interruption, she carries out every signed note again from the start, and ignores an unsigned one.

A **journal** is that notebook. The file system groups the writes of one change into a transaction, which must happen completely or not at all. It writes every changed block to a log area of its own (inode 8, 4 MB in the Try it's image), then a commit record, the signature. Only then does it copy those blocks to their real places, a step called checkpointing. After a crash, mounting the file system (connecting it so programs can use it) replays each transaction that has a commit record and ignores the one that doesn't. That takes about as long as reading the journal. The figure shows the order.

By default ext4 journals only metadata, the facts about files (inodes, bitmaps, directories), and not the bytes in them. In this mode, `data=ordered`, its documentation says a file's new data goes to its place on the disk before the metadata that points at it is committed. So after a crash, an inode never points at a block that still holds another file's old bytes. ext4 commits at least every 5 seconds (`commit=5`).

Keep the last lesson's rule next to this one. A journal makes the file system's structure survive a crash, and nothing more. Data you wrote without `fsync`, the call that waits until the disk has a file's data, can still be missing afterwards. A file can even come back shorter than your last `write()` left it.

The lab builds the three tables as a small model.

Two `open` calls make two descriptions, each starting at 0, and the later writer wins. Add `O_APPEND` to the opens on the right and you get the left side's result, because the kernel then moves each description to the end of the file before every write.

worked.title: Find what holds a deleted file and free the space

steps.say: Start from the symptom. A file system is full, and `du` over it adds up to far less than `df` says is in use. The gap is blocks that no name reaches. Here it's the whole 41 MB.
steps.code:
df -m /dev/shm
# Filesystem     1M-blocks  Used Available Use% Mounted on
# shm                   64    41        24  63% /dev/shm
du -sm /dev/shm
# 0	/dev/shm

steps.say: Find the program that holds them. `lsof +L1` lists open files with a link count below 1. Without `lsof`, search every process's fd entries in `/proc` for `(deleted)`.

# java     33 root    4w   REG  0,179 41943200     0    2 /dev/shm/auth.log (deleted)
find /proc/[0-9]*/fd -lname '*(deleted)' 2>/dev/null
# /proc/33/fd/4

steps.say: Check how the file was opened before you truncate it. In `fdinfo`, the `flags` are written in octal (base 8): `01` is `O_WRONLY` (write only) and `02000` is `O_APPEND`. With `O_APPEND`, the writer's next line goes to the new end. Without it, the line lands at the old offset and leaves a gap of zeros.
Keep a copy if you need the contents, then truncate through `/proc`. The blocks are freed at once, and the program keeps running and logging.
Then fix the cause. Whatever deleted the file should truncate or rename it instead, and the program should open a new file when its log is rotated.

lab.title: Build a file system with inodes, links and shared offsets
steps: Read `FileSystem.kt`. It models the three tables: `Inode`, `OpenFile` (the open file description) and `Proc` (a process and its fd table). Path lookup, `mkdir`, `symlink`, `rename`, `read`, `dup2`, `exit`, `dfBlocks` and `duBlocks` are written for you. So are the private helpers you'll call: `parent` (the directory and last name of a path), `newInode`, `desc` (the description behind an fd), `release` and `dropName`.
Run the tests from the `labs` folder. All eleven fail, because the methods you'll write aren't there yet.
Write `link` and `unlink`. A name is an entry in a directory's `entries` map, and the inode keeps the count in `links`.

Write `open` and `close`. `open` refuses with `EMFILE` at the limit, creates the file when it's given `CREATE`, makes a new `OpenFile` and takes the lowest free fd. `close` frees the description when its last reference goes, and then maybe the inode.
Write `write` and `fork`. Three tests replay the three runs of `share.c` and check against its real output, offsets included.
hints: `fork` must put the same `OpenFile` object in the child's table and add one to its `refs`. A copy of the object would give the child its own offset, which is what `open` does.

In `write`, handle `APPEND` first: set the offset to `data.length`, then write. `StringBuilder.replace(start, end, text)` writes over the text from `start`, and grows the builder when the new text runs past the end.
Lower `inode.openFiles` only when a description's `refs` reaches 0, then call `release`. That's what keeps a deleted file alive while any process holds it.
The lowest free fd: start at 0 and count up while `fd in p.fds`.

drill.title: Draw the tables after a fork and a second open
drill.prompt: A process opens `ledger.csv` and gets fd 3. It forks, and then the child opens `ledger.csv` again and gets fd 4. The child writes 10 bytes to fd 3 and 5 bytes to fd 4, and then the parent writes 7 bytes to fd 3. None of the opens used `O_APPEND`. From memory, write down how many open file descriptions exist, which fds point at each, each description's offset at the end, and the file's size.

answer.src:
descriptions: 2
  D1 (the parent's open, before fork): parent fd 3, child fd 3   refs 2
  D2 (the child's second open):       child fd 4                 refs 1

child writes 10 bytes on fd 3  -> D1 offset 0 -> 10
child writes  5 bytes on fd 4  -> D2 offset 0 -> 5   (over bytes 0-4)
parent writes 7 bytes on fd 3  -> D1 offset 10 -> 17

end: D1 offset 17, D2 offset 5, file size 17
one inode, link count 1, open descriptions 2

recap: A file is an inode: its size, owner, permissions, times, link count and the blocks that hold its data, with a number and no name. A directory is a list of names, each pointing at an inode number.

A hard link is a second name for the same inode, and a symlink is an inode of its own that holds a path. `rm` removes one name, and the kernel frees the file only when no names and no open descriptions are left.

Three tables lead from a program to a file: its fd table points at open file descriptions (one per `open()`, each with an offset), which point at the inode. `fork` shares a description, a second `open()` makes a new one, and `O_APPEND` sends every write to the end so writers don't overwrite each other.
A deleted file that's still open keeps its space: `df` counts it and `du` doesn't. Find it with `lsof +L1` or `/proc/<pid>/fd`, and truncate it instead of restarting the program.

Every open file and network connection is a descriptor. A leak ends in "Too many open files" (`EMFILE`) at the process's limit, or `ENFILE` at the machine's, and the JVM raises its soft limit to the hard one, so a high limit only delays the failure.
The limit of today's tools: a journal keeps the file system's own records consistent through a power cut, and nothing more. Data you wrote without `fsync` can still be lost.
closing:
We started with a disk that stayed full after its biggest file was deleted. The name was gone, but the payments program still held the file open, and the kernel never frees a file that a program still holds.

On a Linux computer you can reach, run `lsof +L1` to look for deleted files that are still open, and `ls /proc/<pid>/fd | wc -l` to count one program's descriptors. On a Mac, `lsof -p <pid>` lists a program's open files and network connections side by side.

Next, we'll look at what a program does while it waits for bytes that haven't arrived yet, and how one program can wait on thousands of connections at once.

quiz.q: From Processes: fork, exec, wait and signals. A shell runs `(date; hostname) > out.txt`, which runs two programs one after the other and sends what they print to `out.txt`. Why does the file end up with both lines, instead of `hostname` writing over `date`?
options: The shell opens `out.txt` with `O_APPEND`, so every write goes to the end
Both programs get an fd 1 that points at the one open file description the shell made, so they share its offset
The kernel always writes at the end of a file that two processes have open
The shell collects both outputs and writes them once at the end
quiz.why: The shell opens the file once, and each program gets fd 1 through `fork`, pointing at the same description, so the second program starts where the first one stopped. The first option is the tempting one, but `>` opens the file with `O_TRUNC` (empty it first), not `O_APPEND`; that's what `>>` does. The kernel doesn't append on its own: two separate `open()` calls overwrite each other, as `share.c` showed. And the shell doesn't collect its children's output.

quiz.q: On a server, `df` says the file system holding `/var`, the folder where programs keep their logs, is 98% full. But `du -sh /var` adds up to only 30 GB of its 100 GB. What's the most likely explanation, and the first command to run?
options: The file system is damaged; run `fsck` to repair it
The journal has grown to 70 GB; make it smaller
Deleted files are still held open by running programs; run `lsof +L1`
`du` doesn't count files larger than 4 GB; use `ls -l` instead
quiz.why: `df` counts blocks in use, and `du` counts what names reach. A large gap means blocks that no name reaches, which is almost always files deleted while a program holds them open. `lsof +L1` lists them, and truncating through `/proc/<pid>/fd/<n>` frees the space. A damaged file system doesn't hide 70 GB this way. The journal has a fixed size (4 MB in the Try it's image, a few hundred MB at most on large disks), and `du` counts big files fine.

quiz.q: `/data` holds `rates.csv`, a hard link to it named `rates-backup.csv`, and a symlink `rates-latest.csv` that points to `rates.csv`, all in the same directory. A job runs `mv rates.csv archive/`, which moves the file into the `archive` folder on the same file system. Which names still open the data?
options: `archive/rates.csv` and `rates-backup.csv`; the symlink now leads nowhere
All three: links follow the file wherever it moves
Only `archive/rates.csv`
`archive/rates.csv` and `rates-latest.csv`; the hard link broke
quiz.why: Within one file system, `mv` is a rename: it moves a directory entry, and the inode stays as it was. The hard link holds the inode's number, so it still works. The symlink holds the path `rates.csv`, and that name no longer exists in `/data`, so it leads nowhere. The second option is tempting because the moved file is still the same file. But only names that hold its inode number can reach it.

quiz.q: The team that runs a Java program sets `ulimit -S -n 1024` for it, a soft limit of 1,024 open descriptors. The program leaks descriptors, yet it fails with "Too many open files" only after about a million. Why?
options: The kernel ignores soft limits
The JVM raises its soft limit to the hard limit when it starts, so only the hard limit applies
Each Java stream uses 1,000 kernel descriptors
Network connections don't count against the limit
quiz.why: The soft limit is the one the kernel enforces, which rules out the first option. But any process may raise its soft limit up to the hard limit, and the JVM does exactly that at start-up (`MaxFDLimit`, on by default; `strace` shows the `prlimit64` call). The leak then runs until the hard limit, or until the machine's `fs.file-max`. Network connections are descriptors and count like files.

quiz.q: From The page cache, writeback and fsync. A program appends records to a file with `write()` and no `fsync`. Two seconds later the power fails. The file system is ext4 in `data=ordered` mode, and after the restart it's ready in a second, with no `fsck`. What can you expect?
options: The file is exactly as the last `write()` left it: the journal kept it safe
The file system may need a full `fsck` before it can be used
The file system is consistent, but the file may be missing its last records or be shorter
The file is lost entirely, because the journal throws away files that were open
quiz.why: The journal replays the committed changes to metadata, so the file system's structure is consistent and no `fsck` is needed. But it journals metadata only, and ext4 commits at most every 5 seconds, while new data waits up to 30 seconds in memory before it's written to the disk. Records that only reached the page cache, the kernel's copy of file data in memory, are gone, and the file's size may go back to the last committed change. The first option is the trap: only `fsync` makes data durable.

flashcards.front: What does an inode hold, and what doesn't it hold?
flashcards.back: The file's type, size, owner, permissions, times, link count and where its data blocks are. Not its name: names live in directories.

flashcards.front: Hard link or symlink: which one still works after the original name is renamed?
flashcards.back: The hard link, because it holds the inode number. A symlink holds a path, which leads nowhere once that name is gone.

flashcards.front: When does the kernel free a deleted file's blocks?
flashcards.back: When its link count is 0 and no open file description points at it: after the last program that has it open closes it.

flashcards.front: What's in an open file description?
flashcards.back: The offset (where the next read or write happens), the flags the file was opened with, such as `O_APPEND`, and a pointer to the inode. Each `open()` makes one; `fork` and `dup2` share it.

flashcards.front: Why does `O_APPEND` stop two writers from overwriting each other?
flashcards.back: Before each write, the kernel sets the offset to the end of the file, in the same step as the write.

flashcards.front: `df` says 80 GB used, `du` says 30 GB. Where's the rest?
flashcards.back: Usually in deleted files that programs still have open. `lsof +L1` finds them.
`EMFILE`: this process reached its own limit on open descriptors. `ENFILE`: the whole machine reached its limit, `fs.file-max`.

terms.plain: The record of one file: its type, size, owner, permissions, times, link count and the blocks that hold its data. It has a number, not a name.
One name in a directory (a folder), paired with an inode number.
A second directory entry for the same inode. The inode's link count says how many there are.
A small inode whose content is a path. The kernel looks the path up again each time the link is opened.
The small number a program gets back from open(). It's an entry in the process's fd table that points at an open file description.
What one open() call creates: the offset, the flags and a pointer to the inode. fork and dup2 share it.
The limit on how many descriptors one process may hold open: a soft value the kernel enforces, and a hard ceiling for raising it.
A log area where a file system writes a change and a commit record before it makes the change, so a crash leaves either the old state or the new one.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate deleted the payments program's 20 GB log, and the disk stayed full until the program restarted that night. They ask you why. Explain it, and say what they should do next time.
explain_back.answer: A file on Linux is an inode, a record of the file's size, owner and blocks, and its name is only an entry in a directory that points at that inode. `rm` removed the entry and brought the link count to 0. But the kernel frees an inode and its blocks only when no program has the file open either. The payments program still had the log open: its file descriptor points at an open file description, which points at the inode. So the 20 GB stayed in use, the program kept writing into a file nobody could see by name, and `df` and `du` disagreed. The restart closed the descriptor, and that's when the space came back. Next time, truncate the file instead of deleting it, with `: > app.log`. That frees the blocks at once and leaves the program's descriptor working. If the file is already deleted, `lsof +L1` shows which program holds it, and truncating `/proc/<pid>/fd/<n>` frees it without a restart. If the program opened its log with `O_APPEND`, its next line goes to the start of the empty file; without it, the line lands at the old offset behind a gap of zeros. And whatever cleans up logs should rename or truncate them, so the logging library can move on to a new file.

deeper.body:
A file system can run out of inodes before it runs out of space. ext4 makes a fixed number of them when you create the file system with `mkfs` (16,384 for the 64 MB image in the last Try it, one per 4 KB block in a small image). A disk full of tiny files, such as a cache that writes one file per key, can show free blocks in `df -h` and still refuse new files with `ENOSPC` ("no space left on device"). `df -i` shows inode use. XFS, another common Linux file system, creates inodes as it needs them, so it rarely hits this. Like ext4, it journals changes to metadata, not file data. It also splits its disk into allocation groups, regions that each manage their own free space, so many parts of a program working at once can allocate space without waiting for each other.

Small files have their own tricks. The symlink in the Try it had `Blockcount: 0`: ext4 stores a target shorter than 60 bytes inside the inode itself (a "fast symlink"). And a file can have holes. Writing at offset 1 GB in an empty file makes its size 1 GB, but blocks are given out only where data was written; `ls -l` shows the size and `du` shows the blocks. That's the gap a writer without `O_APPEND` leaves after you truncate its file under it.

The rule that keeps a deleted file alive can work for you on purpose. A program can create a temporary file, open it and `unlink` it at once. Nobody else can open it by name, and the kernel frees it when the program closes it, even if the program crashes. Linux also has a direct way to make a file that never has a name: `open(dir, O_TMPFILE | O_RDWR)` creates an unnamed inode in that directory's file system. You can write it and `fsync` it, and if you decide to keep it, give it a name with `linkat` from `/proc/self/fd/<n>`. It's another way to publish a complete file in one step, next to the write-a-copy-and-rename pattern from The page cache, writeback and fsync.

For ext4's journal itself, `/proc/fs/jbd2/<device>/info` prints how many transactions committed and how long they took. The mount option `data=journal` puts file data through the journal too: every block is written twice, and a small file is fully consistent after a crash. Almost nobody runs it, because the double writes cost speed.
